slides.title: Non-Modifying Algorithms
slides.prompt: Non-modifying algorithms inspect sequence elements without modifying them. Common examples include std::find, std::count, std::for_each, and logical predicate checks like std::all_of.

slides.title: Counting Elements
slides.prompt: Fill in the algorithm function used to count occurrences of a value in a sequence.

slides.title: std::find_if Behavior
slides.prompt: What does std::find_if return when a matching element is found?
options: An iterator pointing to the first element satisfying the predicate
The index integer of the matching element
A copy of the matched object
slides.correctAnswer: An iterator pointing to the first element satisfying the predicate

slides.title: Checking All Conditions
slides.prompt: Fill in the algorithm function returning true if a predicate evaluates to true for all elements in a range.
slides.codeSnippet: bool allEven = std::___(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x){ return x % 2 == 0; });

slides.title: std::none_of Logic
options: When NO elements in the range satisfy the specified predicate condition
When the container is completely empty
When at least one element fails the predicate condition
When all elements satisfy the predicate condition
slides.correctAnswer: When NO elements in the range satisfy the specified predicate condition

slides.title: Counting with Predicate
slides.prompt: Fill in the function used to count elements that meet a condition.
slides.codeSnippet: int evens = std::___(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x){ return x % 2 == 0; });

slides.title: std::for_each Return Value
slides.prompt: What does the std::for_each algorithm return upon completion?
options: The unary function/lambda object passed into it
The total count of iterated elements
slides.correctAnswer: The unary function/lambda object passed into it

slides.title: Mismatch Search
slides.prompt: Fill in the algorithm that compares two ranges and returns a pair of iterators to the first differing elements.

slides.title: std::search vs std::find
slides.prompt: How does std::search differ from std::find?
options: std::search looks for a sub-sequence pattern inside a range; std::find searches for a single value
std::search works only on binary trees
std::find works only on sorted ranges
std::search is faster because it performs binary search
slides.correctAnswer: std::search looks for a sub-sequence pattern inside a range; std::find searches for a single value

slides.title: Checking Any Condition
slides.prompt: Fill in the algorithm returning true if at least one element satisfies a predicate.
slides.codeSnippet: bool hasOdd = std::___(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x){ return x % 2 != 0; });
